raw_case_text:
A 2-and-a-half-year-old native girl was referred to us with 3 days history of fever, diarrhea, and passing out worms in her stools. According to the World Health Organization growth chart, she was identified as severely malnourished with both height and weight-for-age below third centile, corresponding to the 50th percentile of a 6-month-old child. She had no known chronic medical illness or allergy and had received all immunizations as per the national schedule. However, the child is living with only basic amenities and lacks access to safe tap water or basic sanitation.
On admission, intravenous fluid therapy was initiated for mild dehydration. She was also empirically started on intravenous ampicillin and metronidazole for her enterocolitis. Oral albendazole was given for deworming. Her stool, urine, and blood cultures had no growth of pathogens. On the seventh day of hospitalization, she developed a high-grade fever with massive, tender hepatomegaly but had no cardiorespiratory instability. Her white cell counts (38 x 103/microL), eosinophil counts (6 x 103/microL), and C-reactive proteins (80 mg/L) were markedly raised. An urgent abdominal ultrasound showed the presence of multiple hypoechoic lesions with internal echoes suggestive of non-liquefied abscesses at segment VIII and segment V of the liver as shown in Figure 1. There was also disseminated worm infestation within the bowel, liver, and biliary system. Her repeated peripheral blood culture grew Elizabethkingia meningoseptica, which was identified by the Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry (MS). The disk diffusion method revealed that the bacteria is sensitive to vancomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, and erythromycin. Antibiotics were escalated to intravenous imipenem/cilastatin in suspicion of possible disseminated melioidosis which was highly endemic in the area and intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was also added for treatment of her Elizabethkingia meningoseptica bacteremia. After 72 hours following this combination of antibiotic therapy, her blood culture showed clearance of the organism and there was also an improvement in her septic parameters: white cell counts (26 x 103/microL), eosinophil counts (6 x 103/microL), and C-reactive proteins (18 mg/L) with lower temperature spikes. A repeated ultrasound of the liver after a week of antibiotics showed liver abscesses at segment VIII and segment V which were liquefied. After consultation with the pediatric surgical team, percutaneous drainage of the liver abscesses with pigtail insertion was done under ultrasound guidance by the interventional radiologist. However, only minimal pus was drained during the procedure and the pigtail was removed after 72 hours. She remained afebrile after surgical drainage. The pus culture had no growth of any organism. She was treated with 6 weeks of intravenous imipenem/cilastatin. On the other hand, intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was changed to oral therapy after a week to continue for 2 months.
She was followed up at our pediatric clinic after completion of antibiotics. She remained well with good weight gain. Her weight had improved to achieve 10th centile for her age. Her repeated ultrasound abdomen showed resolving liver lesions with calcifications as shown in Figure 2. Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture of the pus and serum melioidosis serology were otherwise negative.
A newborn premature baby girl was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery at the post-conceptional age of 27 weeks 1 day, with an extremely low body weight of 870 g. She was apneic and bradycardic at birth, rendering her to be intubated at 5 minutes of life due to poor respiratory effort. Subsequently, she was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit. She had severe respiratory distress syndrome requiring ventilation with high-frequency oscillatory ventilation and received 2 doses of intratracheal beractant. Her umbilical artery and vein were cannulated at birth. She was also empirically covered with intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin for presumed neonatal sepsis. Total parenteral nutrition was also commenced at 2 hours of life via the umbilical vein catheter.
On her fourth day of life, she developed nosocomial pneumonia evidenced by frequent desaturation with worsening alveolar infiltrates on her chest X-ray. The antibiotics were escalated to intravenous ceftazidime and amikacin. Despite this, she continued to develop leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 42 x 103/microL and thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 45 x 103/microL on the sixth day of life. Her C-reactive protein was raised at 17 mg/dL. Peripheral blood culture isolated a Gram-negative bacteria identified as Elizabethkingia anopheles by MALDI-TOF MS, which was sensitive to vancomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampicin, and ciprofloxacin based on the disk diffusion method. The cerebrospinal fluid analysis was not suggestive of meningitis and culture was negative. Bedside cranial ultrasound showed left grade 1 intraventricular hemorrhage without any ventriculomegaly. She was commenced on a combination of intravenous vancomycin and ciprofloxacin.
Peripheral blood culture was repeated after 48 hours of treatment. However, there was persistent growth of the same organism with no improvement in her blood counts. Hence, the decision was made to withhold her total parenteral nutrition and remove both umbilical catheters. A pediatric infectious disease specialist was consulted, and the antibiotics were revised to a combination of intravenous vancomycin and oral rifampicin. Subsequent blood culture at 72 hours after removing the umbilical catheters was sterile, normalizing her platelet and white cell counts. Her c-reactive protein had also reduced to 3 mg/dL. Both intravenous vancomycin and oral rifampicin were continued for a total of 2 weeks.
She was successfully extubated on her 10th day of life but had moderate bronchopulmonary dysplasia. She had bilateral stage 1 retinopathy of prematurity and her cranial ultrasound prior to discharge was normal. She was discharged home on day 115 of life and continued to follow up at our pediatric clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2.5-year-old native girl presented with a 3-day history of fever, diarrhea, and passing worms in her stools (Case 1); the report also describes a newborn premature baby girl born at 27 weeks 1 day gestation with an extremely low birth weight of 870 g presenting with apnea, bradycardia, and severe respiratory distress syndrome at birth (Case 2).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In Case 1, the 2.5-year-old girl developed fever, diarrhea, and passage of worms in her stools for 3 days prior to referral. In Case 2, the premature female neonate was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery at post-conceptional age 27 weeks 1 day (birth weight 870 g), was apneic and bradycardic at birth requiring endotracheal intubation at 5 minutes of life for poor respiratory effort, and was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with severe respiratory distress syndrome.
subjective.past_medical_history: Case 1: Severely malnourished with height and weight-for-age below the 3rd centile (corresponding to the 50th percentile of a 6-month-old child) on the WHO growth chart; no known chronic medical illness; immunizations up to date per the national schedule; lived with basic amenities lacking access to safe tap water or basic sanitation. Case 2: Preterm birth at 27 weeks 1 day gestation with extremely low birth weight (870 g); umbilical artery and vein cannulated at birth and total parenteral nutrition commenced at 2 hours of life.
subjective.review_of_systems: Case 1: Positive for fever, diarrhea, and helminth passage in stool; no known allergies. Case 2: Positive for neonatal apnea, bradycardia, and poor respiratory effort at birth.

objective.physical_examination: Case 1: Mild dehydration and severe malnutrition (height and weight-for-age <3rd centile) on admission; on day 7 of hospitalization, she developed a high-grade fever and massive, tender hepatomegaly without cardiorespiratory instability. Case 2: Apneic and bradycardic at birth with poor respiratory effort; on day 4 of life, she had frequent oxygen desaturations.
objective.routine_investigations: Case 1: Initial stool, urine, and blood cultures had no pathogen growth. On day 7, white cell count was 38 x 10^3/microL, eosinophil count was 6 x 10^3/microL, and C-reactive protein (CRP) was 80 mg/L. Urgent abdominal ultrasound showed multiple hypoechoic lesions with internal echoes suggestive of non-liquefied abscesses at liver segments VIII and V, along with disseminated worm infestation within the bowel, liver, and biliary system. After 72 hours of escalated antibiotics, repeat WBC was 26 x 10^3/microL, eosinophil count was 6 x 10^3/microL, and CRP was 18 mg/L. Repeat liver ultrasound after 1 week showed liquefied abscesses at segments VIII and V. Case 2: Day 4 chest X-ray showed worsening alveolar infiltrates. On day 6 of life, WBC was 42 x 10^3/microL, platelet count was 45 x 10^3/microL, and CRP was 17 mg/dL (later reducing to 3 mg/dL after catheter removal and antibiotic revision). Bedside cranial ultrasound showed left grade 1 intraventricular hemorrhage without ventriculomegaly (normal prior to discharge).
objective.advanced_workup: Case 1: Disk diffusion antimicrobial susceptibility testing of the peripheral blood isolate (Elizabethkingia meningoseptica) demonstrated sensitivity to vancomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, and erythromycin. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage of the liver abscesses with pigtail catheter insertion yielded minimal pus with sterile pus culture. Case 2: Disk diffusion testing of the blood isolate (Elizabethkingia anophelis) showed sensitivity to vancomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampicin, and ciprofloxacin. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was not suggestive of meningitis and CSF culture was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnoses: Case 1 was diagnosed with Elizabethkingia meningoseptica bacteremia (identified via MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry from repeated peripheral blood culture), disseminated helminthiasis, and multiple liver abscesses (melioidosis and tuberculosis were ruled out via negative serum melioidosis serology and negative Mycobacterium tuberculosis pus culture). Case 2 was diagnosed with catheter-related Elizabethkingia anophelis bacteremia (identified via MALDI-TOF MS) and nosocomial pneumonia complicated by moderate bronchopulmonary dysplasia and bilateral stage 1 retinopathy of prematurity. Treatment and outcome: Case 1 initially received IV fluids, empiric IV ampicillin, IV metronidazole, and oral albendazole; on day 7, therapy was escalated to IV imipenem/cilastatin (for suspected endemic melioidosis, continued for 6 weeks) and IV trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (for E. meningoseptica, switched after 1 week to oral therapy for 2 months), alongside ultrasound-guided pigtail drainage for 72 hours. Her blood cultures cleared within 72 hours, she remained afebrile, achieved the 10th weight centile at clinic follow-up, and repeat ultrasound showed resolving calcified liver lesions. Case 2 initially received high-frequency oscillatory ventilation, 2 doses of intratracheal beractant, and empiric IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, escalated on day 4 to IV ceftazidime and amikacin, then IV vancomycin and ciprofloxacin; due to persistent bacteremia at 48 hours, total parenteral nutrition was withheld, both umbilical catheters were removed, and therapy was revised to IV vancomycin and oral rifampicin for 2 weeks, achieving blood culture sterility at 72 hours, extubation on day 10 of life, and discharge home on day 115 of life.
